1:
Two place the verse in the argument before doing anything else with it. Augustine of Hippo reminds his hearers where the previous day’s exposition stopped, at the man who cannot love the God he has not seen if he does not love the brother he has, reading this sentence as continuing that thought. His question is not who believes but who does not: the man who does not believe that Jesus is the Christ is the man who does not live as Christ commanded, since many say I believe and faith without works does not save, the work of faith being love. He then presses the point with a figure of running. Works done before believing were either none, in which case a man was footless or too sore-footed to walk, or else they seemed good, in which case he ran but ran aside from the road and went astray instead of arriving; so we must both run and run in the way. Barnes, whose block here is an analysis of the whole chapter, agrees that the first three verses continue the discussion of love and belong with the previous chapter. Henry sets the verse as a third reason for brotherly love: it is demanded by the eminent relation of those loved, fellow-believers being nearly related to God as his children. The brother is described by his faith and dignified by his descent; and Henry draws the consequence that sonship is no longer appropriated to the seed of Abraham after the flesh, since all believers are spiritually descended from God and to be loved accordingly.

What believing that Jesus is the Christ amounts to is drawn from the title. Gill takes the word to mean anointed and so to cover every office to which the Son was anointed, so that to believe him the Christ is to believe him the prophet Moses promised, the priest after the order of Melchizedek, and the king. Calvin adds why the title matters: it designates the office to which he was appointed by the Father, so that to believe he is the Christ is to hope from him everything promised of the Messiah, and he cannot be received as Christ unless salvation is sought from him. Cyril of Jerusalem locates the exact point of denial: that he is Jesus the Jews allow, but not that he is Christ, which is why the Apostle asks who is the liar but he that denies it; and he expounds a priesthood passing to no successor, held not by bodily descent nor by oil prepared by man but by appointment before all ages. Robertson identifies the contemporary denial, that the antichrist of this letter separates Jesus from the Christ, and insists that what John requires is not intellectual conviction but full surrender to him as Lord and Saviour. Clarke joins the two halves of the verse: he who believes Jesus to be the Messiah and confides in him for remission is begotten of God, and those pardoned and begotten love him in return and love all who are his children.

Which comes first, believing or begetting, is answered oppositely. Robertson quotes with approval the judgment that the divine begetting is the antecedent and not the consequent of the believing, and Calvin says the same, that all who really believe have been born of God, faith being far above the reach of nature; Clarke runs the other way, making the begetting follow on the believing. Robertson also parses the closing participles, the one who begat being the Father and the one begotten the brother by that same Father, so that we prove our love for the Father by our conduct toward them; and Wesley takes the scope of the paragraph from its conclusion, observing that faith is the first and last point with this apostle and that whoever loves the Father has a natural affection to all his brethren.
2: The direction of the test is what strikes them, because it runs the opposite way from the usual one. Barnes states it as a reversal: elsewhere the apostle says we may know we love God if we love those who bear his image, and here he says there is another way of determining what we are, since we may have evidence of loving God apart from our conduct toward Christians — consciousness of it, pleasure in meditating on his perfections, the certainty of being moved to obey him as a child is moved toward a father — and from that, as the basis of an argument, we may infer true love to his children. He raises the obvious objection himself, that surely love to Christians is easier to ascertain than love to God, and answers that men may love Christians from many motives, as personal friends and for other reasons that are not religious at all. Robertson reaches the same result by a different route, quoting the judgment that the love of God and the love of the brethren each include the other, so that each is a test of the other, and putting this verse alongside the earlier one that runs the other way. He notes the indefinite temporal construction, whenever we keep on loving God and whenever we keep on doing his commandments. Calvin explains why the test needs stating in this direction at all: it often happens that we love men apart from God, since unholy and carnal friendships regard only private advantage or some other vanishing object, so that having first given the effect the apostle now gives the cause, and mutual love must be cultivated in such a way that God is honoured. Clarke compresses the whole into a chain, that our love of God’s followers proves we love God, our love to God is the cause of our loving his children, and our keeping his commandments is the proof that we love him. Gill flags a version that turns the clause into a tautology, making it prove the same by the same, where the apostle’s point is to show when love to the saints is right. Wesley calls the verse a plain proof.
3:
On the commandments themselves Calvin joins two things that might be separated: to love God as Father and Lord is necessarily to reverence him, and since God cannot be divided from himself, and is the fountain of all righteousness, whoever loves him must have a heart prepared to obey righteousness — the love of God being neither idle nor inactive. He also enters a caution about what obedience means, that if we keep the commandments only under constraint of fear we are very far from true obedience. Gill takes the keeping as evidence that love is not in word and tongue only but in deed and truth, and adds that those who so act have a sense of God’s love on their souls and may expect greater manifestations of it. Robertson calls obedience the supreme test and reads the construction as explanatory, showing what the love of God is as against mere declamatory boasting.

Whether the commandments are in fact not grievous is where the difficulty is felt, and only one of them meets it head on. Barnes says the word means heavy, difficult to bear as a burden, and that the laws are not unreasonable nor beyond our ability; complaints of that kind come only from those not disposed to keep them, and no true Christian ever called the laws of God stern or grievous, since the service of God is freedom and the service of the world is bondage. Clarke says the same through a proverb, that love feels no loads, since no man is burdened with the duties his own love imposes, and adds that love to God brings strength from God, so that the commandments become not merely light but delightful; he quotes a rabbinic saying that a man can bring God no other worship than love. Robertson puts it in five words, that love for God lightens his commands. Wesley adds the qualification the others leave implicit, that they are not grievous to any that are born of God. Calvin alone states the objection in full: we have found it far otherwise by experience, and Scripture itself testifies that the yoke of the law is insupportable; since self-denial is the prelude to keeping the law, and since the law is spiritual while we are flesh, there must be great discord between us and it. His answer is that the difficulty arises not from the nature of the law but from our corrupt flesh, which is how he reconciles the apostle who makes the law a master of death with the psalmist who delights in it.
4:
The neuter of the opening phrase is noticed by four of them and read the same way. Robertson says the neuter singular participle is used instead of the masculine to express sharply the universality of the principle; Calvin agrees that the neuter stands for the masculine, reports the view that it was chosen to take in all sorts of persons — male and female, young and old, Jew and Gentile, bond and free — and then declines it, asking why the neuter was not used in the first verse and concluding that it is a peculiarity of style and nothing else, not to be preserved in translation. Wesley reads it as implying the most unlimited universality, and Clarke notes the same grammatical substitution. Barnes puts the substance rather than the form: the phrase means that in every instance of true regeneration there is this victory, so that where the spirit of the world reigns supreme in the heart there is no true religion — from which he draws the uncomfortable inference about how many professed Christians are wholly governed by that spirit. Gill allows the words to cover either the persons born of God or the new creature and principle of grace wrought in them, faith in particular.

What the world means gets one uncommon answer. Clarke reports the opinion that it stands here for the Jewish Church or Judaism, which was often called this world, on two grounds: that it was this world which denied the Messiah had come, the Gentiles not opposing that principle, and that the apostle argues against the Jews in a Jewish manner, so that the sense would be that a man who holds the true Christian faith can easily convict the Jewish religion of falsity. He then offers the ordinary reading as an alternative, that the world means the evil principles and practices found among men and in the human heart, over which the influence of God in the soul prevails. Robertson defines it as the sum of all the forces antagonistic to the spiritual life, and reads the present tense as a continuous victory because a continuous struggle. Barnes describes the same conflict as one in which religion secures the victory in the heart of every true Christian, the foundation having been laid by Christ’s own triumph.

On the change of tense in the second clause two of them make the same observation and draw slightly different comfort from it. Robertson notes that the aorist participle singles out an individual experience, the moment when one believed or met a temptation with victory, and remarks that English cannot reproduce the play on the word. Calvin fastens on the past tense as more emphatic than either present or future: the apostle speaks as though the enemy had already been put to flight, so that we may feel certain — and he adds that although Satan continually repeats his horrible onsets and our warfare continues through life, the Spirit of God removes fear by declaring us beyond the reach of danger. He also observes that victory here stands for what brings victory, the effect put for the cause. Robertson notes that the noun occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and that the word for faith appears only here in these letters.
5: The closing question is taken by all as an appeal to fact rather than a rhetorical flourish. Robertson says as much explicitly, and finds in the verse a sharp antithesis between the human name and the divine title united in one personality. Gill says the question carries a strong affirmation that no other person is the conqueror of the world, and Wesley answers it in four words, every believer and none else. Barnes presses the appeal at length and grants everything short of the point: a man may subdue some one evil propensity, abandon a gay circle, break from habits of profaneness, exchange the ardent passions of youth for the soberness of middle life, withdraw from politics after a disappointment, or like certain emperors lay down public office when satiated with its pageantry — and still, without faith in the Son of God, the spirit of the world will reign in his soul in some form. Calvin supplies the reason the victory belongs to faith at all: we conquer because we derive strength from Christ, so that only the man who distrusts himself and rests on Christ’s power can overcome; and by faith he means a real apprehension of Christ, an effectual laying hold by which we apply his power to ourselves. Clarke defines the belief in question as belief that Jesus is the promised Messiah who came by a supernatural generation, truly man yet not by man; and he draws out what follows from holding it, that such a person has the privilege of applying to the Lord for the benefits of the incarnation and passion and receives blessings the Jews cannot have, since they do not believe the divine mission of Christ. Barnes puts the same appeal in the form John used it, asking where one may be found who shows that all his purposes in regard to this world are made subordinate to the world to come. He allows that men change with age and circumstance, that ambition is disappointed and gaiety satiated and hearts crushed by loss, and holds that none of it reaches the case; and Robertson notes that the article and participle describe not a single act but the man who keeps on conquering.
6:
What the water is divides them, and the division is clean. Gill states the baptismal reading and clears three others away: the water is not the ablutions of the ceremonial law, nor the purity of Christ’s own nature, nor the cleansing of his people from their sins, which is what he came to do and not what he came by. It is the ordinance of water baptism; and though Christ did not come baptizing, John came baptizing so that he might be made manifest, and it was at Jordan that he was declared Son of God. Clarke reads it the same way and supplies the scene, the Spirit descending and the voice from heaven; he takes the blood for the sacrificial death, so that the Spirit witnessed his sonship at the baptism and had witnessed in the prophets that he should die such a death. Robertson agrees, water at the baptism and blood at the Cross, and explains the choice of these two: at the baptism Jesus was formally set apart to his Messianic work by the Spirit and the Father’s audible witness, and at the Cross the work reached its culmination. Wesley holds both together in one arc: at his baptism he undertook to fulfil all righteousness and on the cross accomplished it, the blood and water from his side being the token that all was finished. Calvin dissents. He grants there is no question about the blood by which Christ reconciled God, but says a reference to baptism is not probable, taking the water from the pierced side instead, which he regards as done by God’s purpose so that Christ’s side might become the fountain of blood and water. His reading of the pair is typological: the apostle alludes to the ancient rites, under which water washed away filth and blood made expiation, and denotes by the two the whole perfection of holiness and righteousness, the proof being that Jesus brought the substance of what the law shadowed.

Why the apostle repeats himself, adding not by water only, is answered from the controversy behind the letter. Robertson notes that both preposition and article are repeated in the second clause, which argues for two separate events with the emphasis on the blood, the thing the Gnostics made light of; and the water and blood from the pierced side refute at once the denial that Jesus had a human body and the distinction drawn between Jesus and the Christ. Barnes reads the verse as a statement of what evidence is on offer, and guards against a misreading: to come by water and blood does not mean Christ was accompanied by them at his coming into the world, but that these were manifest during his appearing and were testimonials to his work.

Henry works the two out as remedies matched to two defilements. Faith so victorious had need to be well founded, and Christ brings his credentials both in the way by which he came and in the witness that attends him, coming by water and blood as the notes of a true Saviour and as the means by which he heals. We are defiled inwardly by the pollution of sin in our nature, for which we need a water able to reach the soul, supplied in the washing of regeneration. Clarke adds a comparison the others do not draw, suggesting Moses and Aaron are in view: Moses came by water, all Israel being baptized to him in the cloud and the sea, and Aaron by blood, entering the holy place with the blood of the victim — between them doing what Christ does alone. Wesley closes on the third witness, that the Spirit testifies of Christ by Moses and the prophets, by the Baptist and the apostles, and that against it there can be no exception, the Spirit being the very God of truth.
7:
No verse here is treated at such length, and the corpus splits three ways over whether it belongs to the text at all. Barnes says no passage in the New Testament has produced so much discussion, and identifies why: the testimony the words seem to bear to the Trinity has made the part of the Church holding that doctrine unwilling to give them up and those who deny it equally unwilling to admit them. He brackets the disputed words so the reader may see what the passage reads like without them, then gives his reasons for judging them spurious, beginning with the manuscripts: the clause is in no Greek copy written before the sixteenth century. Clarke reaches the same verdict and gives the count: the words are wanting in every manuscript written before printing except one at Dublin, the copies omitting them amounting to a hundred and twelve, and wanting in every ancient version but the Latin, in many of the oldest copies even of that, and in all the ancient Greek fathers. Like Barnes he prints the passage twice, once as the Greek manuscripts have it and once with the addition bracketed. Robertson is the bluntest. The words stand in no Greek manuscript except two late cursives; the editor of the first printed Greek Testament did not have them, rashly offered to insert them if a single Greek manuscript could be produced, and had one produced as if made to order. His reconstruction is that a Latin scribe caught up an early exegesis and wrote it in his margin, whence it passed into the Latin version and finally into the received text; and he adds the point that matters most to him, that neither the fact nor the doctrine of the Trinity depends on the addition.

Gill argues the other way and answers the objections one at a time. He grants that the verse is wanting in the Syriac, Arabic and Ethiopic versions, that the old Latin interpreter has it not, that many Greek manuscripts lack it, and that many ancient fathers do not cite it, even those writing against the Arians where it would have served them. To the first he replies that the Syriac, however ancient, is only a version and a defective one, since several whole books were formerly wanting in it until supplied from later copies — as this verse has since been supplied from an eastern copy. Wesley defends it too, resting on the critical work of a scholar of his own century concerning both the transposition of these verses and the authority of the disputed one, and elsewhere claiming an uninterrupted train of fathers for it; his estimate of its importance is the highest given here, that this verse is to the epistle what the needle is to the mariner’s compass.

Calvin stands between and declines to decide. He reports that some omit the verse and that one father thought this done by design rather than mistake, and only among the Latins; but since even the Greek copies disagree he dares not assert anything. What inclines him to receive it is not manuscript evidence but two other things, that the passage flows better with the clause and that he finds it in what he takes to be the best copies. The block printed under his name then continues with an argument that the passage is spurious after all, citing the absence of the words from the Greek manuscripts; that material is a later editor’s note rather than Calvin, and it reverses his conclusion instead of continuing it. On the doctrine itself, where none of them differ, Clarke states what the three witnesses do: the Father testifies to the Son, the Word to the Father and the Holy Ghost to both, the three being one in essence and agreeing in one testimony, that Jesus came to die for the world and give it life.
8:
The verse divisions themselves are unsettled here, because the disputed clause straddles the two verses, and the commentators do not all number alike. Barnes says the words in earth are part of what must go if his reasoning holds, since the phrase was introduced only to answer the in heaven of the interpolated sentence; on his text the genuine verse reads simply that there are three that bear record, the Spirit and the water and the blood. Wesley’s comment printed here belongs to the other half of the pair, expounding the Father, the Word and the Spirit as the three that testify in heaven. Robertson takes the clause as it stands as a resumption, the same three witnesses named again with the Spirit placed first, and reads the closing phrase as meaning that they are for the one thing, namely to bring us to faith in Jesus as the incarnate Son of God, which he identifies as the stated purpose of the Fourth Gospel. Gill notes only that they witness to the same truth, the sonship of Christ.

What the three earthly witnesses are is answered by Clarke in words he takes over from Wesley and attributes to him by name: the Spirit in the word confirmed by miracles, the water in baptism, in which we are dedicated to the Son and which typifies his spotless purity and the inward purifying of our nature, and the blood represented in the Lord’s Supper and applied to the consciences of believers — all three agreeing in the same testimony, that Jesus Christ is the divine, the complete and the only Saviour of the world. Clarke then works each out as a witness still bearing testimony now: the written word, proceeding from the Holy Spirit, is that Spirit continually witnessing on earth that God has given us eternal life; baptism, still maintained as an initiatory rite, points to regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Ghost and is another present witness to the truth and efficacy of the Christian religion; and the blood, represented in the eucharist, continues to show forth the death and atoning sacrifice of the Son of God until he comes. Barnes takes the Spirit alone and lists how his witness was given: at the baptism of Jesus, in the endowment of the Messiah with the Spirit’s influences as the prophets had foretold, in the descent on the apostles after the ascension with saving power on thousands, and in the same testimony borne still at every revival of religion and in the conversion of every individual.

Calvin explains why a third witness is added at all, and gives it a rank the verse does not. The water and the blood are the pledges and effects of salvation and testify that Christ was sent by God, so that those who reject him have no excuse; but the Spirit, though named third, holds the first place, since without him the water and blood would have flowed without any benefit. It is he who seals the testimony of the water and blood on our hearts, who by his power makes the fruit of Christ’s death reach us, who makes the blood shed for our redemption penetrate our hearts, and in a word makes Christ with all his blessings ours. He supports this from Paul, who having said that Christ was manifested Son of God by his resurrection adds at once that it was through the sanctification of the Spirit; for whatever signs of divine glory shine out in Christ would remain obscure and escape our sight altogether if the Holy Spirit did not open for us the eyes of faith. That, he concludes, is why the Spirit is adduced as a witness alongside the water and the blood, since it is his peculiar office to cleanse our consciences by the blood of Christ.
9:
The argument is from the less to the greater and everyone treats it so. Calvin states the form: if in worldly affairs we stand by the words of men, who may lie and deceive, how unreasonable that God should be given less credit when he sits as it were on his own throne as supreme judge — so that nothing but our own corruption prevents us receiving Christ, since God has given full proof for believing. Barnes develops the minor premise at length. We are constantly acting on the belief that what others say is true, in families, in the reports of travellers, in books, in courts of justice, and the mind is so made that it must credit the testimony of others; if that credence ceased even for a single day the affairs of the world would come to a pause. Against this he sets what God cannot do: men may be deceived and bear witness unwittingly to what is untrue, may intend to deceive for base purposes, may act on rumours or on partial observation, may desire to excite admiration by the marvellous, and have in fact deceived — and of none of these is God capable. Clarke compresses the whole contrast into a clause, that God can neither be deceived nor deceive while man may do both, and Wesley notes that we accept human testimony continually and must do so in a thousand instances. Henry turns the same comparison into a charge: nothing can be more absurd than the conduct of those who doubt the truth of Christianity while in the common affairs of life they proceed on human testimony without hesitation, and would think a man out of his senses who declined to.

Two of them supply what the human testimony in this particular case consisted of. Gill lists the witnesses actually credited about Christ — the wise men who declared that the King of the Jews was born and that his star had been seen, which even Herod credited enough to summon the chief priests; the shepherds, who reported the appearance of angels and that they had seen the child themselves; and above all the Baptist, whose testimony could not be objected to. Robertson supplies the legal frame instead, that the conditions for a valid witness are laid down in Deuteronomy and appealed to more than once in this Gospel and in Paul, and he passes on the observation that the Trinity appears across these verses in a particular arrangement: the Son comes, the Spirit witnesses, the Father has witnessed. Calvin widens what counts as the divine testimony, so that it means not only what the Spirit imprints on our hearts but also what we derive from the water and the blood, since the power of cleansing and expiating was not earthly but heavenly — from which he draws the rule that the blood of Christ is not to be estimated in the common manner of men but by the design of God, who ordained it for blotting out sins. Wesley identifies the testimony simply as the one the Father with the Word and the Spirit has borne of the Son as Saviour of the world.
10:
What the witness in himself is, and whether it stands apart from the outward evidence, is the question here and it gets two incompatible answers. Barnes rules out one reading before giving his own: the phrase cannot refer to any distinct and immediate revelation of the fact to the soul of the individual, nor is it independent of the external evidence or a substitute for it. The witness he means is the fruit of all the evidence, outward and inward together, working on the heart to produce deep conviction — the peace found by believing, the removal of anxiety on account of sin, the new views of God and heaven, the disarming of death, and the whole influence of the gospel on intellect and life; and this the believer cannot resist, so that he is ready to go to the stake rather than surrender his religion. Clarke takes the other view without qualification: God has witnessed that whoever believes on his Son shall be saved, and the believer has the witness of it in himself, the Spirit bearing witness with his spirit that he is a child of God — to know and feel sin forgiven, and to have the testimony of it in the heart from the Holy Spirit himself, is the privilege of every true believer. Calvin lands nearer Clarke and says why it matters: the apostle does not say that God speaks outwardly, but that every one of the godly feels within that God is the author of his faith, and it is by this that faith is distinguished from a fading opinion which depends on something else — the faithful being beyond the danger of erring because they have God for their foundation.

Henry sets out what the believer can allege, and the list is a catalogue of experience rather than of argument. He has deeply seen his own sin and guilt and misery and his need of such a Saviour; he has seen the excellency and office of the Son of God and how incomparably suited such a Saviour is to his wants; he sees and admires the wisdom and love of God in sending him; he has found and felt the power of Christ’s word wounding, humbling, healing, quickening and comforting his soul; and he finds that the revelation of Christ, being the greatest demonstration of the love of God, is also the most powerful means of kindling love to God in return. Henry adds, in his shorter treatment, that this assurance puts the matter beyond doubt for the believer except in hours of darkness or conflict, and that he cannot be argued out of it. Gill describes the faith in question as believing in Christ for righteousness and eternal life, he being truly and properly God and so able to save all who believe.

On the second half of the verse the note turns severe. Calvin makes the unbeliever guilty of extreme blasphemy, since nothing is more valued by God than his own truth, so that no wrong more atrocious can be done him than to rob him of that honour. Wesley states the mechanism plainly, that such a man supposes to be false what God has expressly testified. Henry says the same in his own idiom, that this is what makes the sin of unbelief so awful, since the unbeliever gives God the lie. Robertson works on the grammar and finds a distinction drawn deliberately: believing God, that is his testimony about his Son, is one thing, and believing on or into the Son, a surrender to him and reliance on him, is another, the two constructions being kept apart in this very verse. He notes that the perfect tenses through the verse describe a permanent state, and that the reason given for the charge is an actual and not merely a supposed one.
11: What the record amounts to is stated the same way by all of them and then developed differently. Barnes calls it the sum or amount of the testimony God has given respecting his Son, that he has provided through the Saviour the means of obtaining eternal life, treasured up in him and to be had through him. Gill takes it as the substance of the record with respect both to the person of Christ and to the security of salvation in him, who is himself the true God and eternal life. Clarke calls it the great truth to which the Spirit, the water and the blood bear testimony, and defines the gift as both a right to endless glory and a meetness for it, coming by and through the Son who is its author and its purchaser, so that no other scheme of salvation can be effectual since God has provided none and a man’s own invention must be vain. Robertson notes the aorist in the clause about the giving, marking the historic fact of the Incarnation, where a perfect is used earlier in the letter to emphasise the abiding presence of God’s love, and observes that the life is anarthrous here and so emphasises quality. Wesley draws out two things the phrase contains at once, that God has given us a title to eternal life and the real beginning of it, both purchased by and treasured up in his Son, who has all the springs and the fulness of it in himself to communicate to his body the church, first in grace and afterwards in glory. Calvin reads the verse as an invitation rather than a statement. Having set forth the benefit, the apostle now invites us to believe; and though it is a reverence due to God to receive whatever he declares as beyond controversy, our ingratitude would be intolerable if we did not receive with prompt faith a doctrine so sweet, since he freely offers life. The point, he says, is that we ought not only to obey the gospel reverently lest we affront God but to love it, because it brings us eternal life; and from this he draws what is especially to be sought in the gospel, namely the free gift of salvation, adding that the exhortations to repentance and fear are not to be separated from the grace of Christ.
12:
The following verse is treated by all as the same truth stated exclusively. Barnes traces it to a saying of the Saviour himself and reads it as the sense of all the important testimony God ever bore on the subject of salvation, that the believer already has the elements of eternal life in his soul and will certainly obtain salvation, while the man who does not believe will not attain it. Gill describes having the Son as a spiritual and experimental knowledge of him and a true faith in him, with Christ dwelling in the heart; and Robertson identifies the life spoken of as the very life God gave in the verse before, and the claim as the one Jesus makes for himself in the Gospel. Clarke presses the exclusion into a rule and warns against evading it: since eternal life is given in the Son it cannot be enjoyed apart from him, so that an indwelling Christ gives both the title and the meetness, and it is vain to expect glory without him. Wesley notices a small change of wording and gives a reason for it: in the first clause the apostle says simply the Son, because believers know him, and in the second the Son of God, so that unbelievers may learn how great a blessing they fall short of. Calvin treats the verse as a deliberate closing of every other door: it might have been enough that God placed life in Christ alone so that it should be sought there, but lest anyone turn aside the apostle shuts out from the hope of life all who do not seek it in him, and shows that everyone separated from the body of Christ is without life — Christ being possessed by faith.

Calvin alone raises the objection that this seems to invite. It looks inconsistent with reason, he says, since history shows great men endowed with heroic virtues who were wholly unacquainted with Christ, and it seems unreasonable that men of such eminence should have no honour. His answer is that we are greatly mistaken if we think whatever is eminent in our eyes is approved by God, and he cites the saying that what is highly esteemed among men is abomination with God; for the filthiness of the heart is hidden from us so that we are satisfied with the external appearance, while God sees what lies concealed beneath it.
13:
What the words refer back to is settled first. Robertson says the aorist is not epistolary but points to the twelve verses just finished, as a similar phrase earlier in the letter points to what precedes it. Gill takes it more widely, of what the epistle contains in general and of the context in particular, the victory over the world, the witnesses to Christ’s sonship, and the record that the gift of eternal life is in him. Barnes reads it as the things written respecting the testimony borne to the Lord Jesus, and glosses believing on the name as believing on the person, the name often standing for the person. Wesley notices the change of tense between the letter’s opening and its close, from I write to I have written.

The purpose clause is where the emphasis falls, and Ellicott measures it against the parallel in the Gospel. There the aim was that they might believe and believing have life; here it is more positive, that they may know they have it, the object being to produce in them a good hope — which he connects to the stated purpose at the beginning of the epistle, the communication of joy through fellowship, since knowing one has eternal life and continuing in faith would be precisely that joy. Robertson notes that the verb for knowing is the one that means settled intuitive knowledge, and adds a caution: the apostle wishes them to have eternal life and to know they have it, but not with flippant superficiality. Wesley makes the same point in a phrase, a fuller and stronger assurance. Barnes reads the second half of the purpose as continuance rather than commencement, since the apostle was sure they already believed; and he turns this into a rule for ministers, that a chief duty is to set the nature and evidences and hopes of religion before real Christians so as to secure their perseverance, since the religious affections grow cold easily even in a converted heart.

Calvin builds the same observation into a doctrine of progress. Since there ought to be daily progress in faith, the apostle writes to people who already believed so that they might believe more firmly and with greater certainty; the use of doctrine, then, is not only to initiate the ignorant in the knowledge of Christ but to confirm those already taught. He puts it sharply: many remnants of unbelief are still in us and our faith is so weak that what we believe is not really believed unless there is fuller confirmation, so we must attend to learning all our lives. And he specifies the means, which is not exhortation in general but exposition in particular — faith is confirmed by having the office and power of Christ explained to us, and it is the duty of a godly teacher to extol these in order to confirm his disciples. Clarke reaches a similar place by another road, saying that he writes to show their privileges and to lead them into the holy of holies, and that believing on the Son of God is known by its effects: not a blind reliance for salvation but an actual enjoyment of it, Christ living and working and reigning in the heart. He then lays the sequence out as a chain — Christ dwells in the heart only by faith, faith lives only by love, love continues only by obedience — so that he who believes loves, he who loves obeys, and he who believes has the witness in himself. Henry states the conclusion the chapter has been building toward, that on all this evidence it is but right we should believe on the name of the Son of God, and that we should thankfully receive the record of Scripture and abound in the work of the Lord, knowing our labour is not in vain.
14:
What the confidence is, and how far it reaches, is defined narrowly by all of them. Barnes says the confidence here relates specifically to the answer to prayer, and is not offered as the only ground of confidence in Christ but as one worthy of special notice, being an effect of believing on him. Gill locates it either in God to whom prayer is made or in the Son through whose blood believers have access, and glosses the word as boldness or liberty of speech, especially where the Spirit is present and the assurance of being heard. Clarke gives the same rendering, liberty of access and of speech, and calls prayer the language of the children of God, spoken by whoever is begotten of him, and the language of dependence, so that where the soul is dumb there is neither life nor love nor faith. Robertson takes the preposition as denoting fellowship face to face with Christ. Calvin makes the boldness itself the chief evidence of faith. Were we shut out from access to God nothing could make us more miserable, but with that refuge open we should be happy even in extreme evils, and this alone makes trouble blessed; so calling on God is the chief trial of our faith, and God is not rightly called upon unless we are fully persuaded our prayers will not be in vain, since the apostle denies faith to those who hesitate in doubt. From this he turns on a whole system of religion in his own day, charging that the doctrine of faith lies buried there because all certainty has been taken away: prayers are muttered and much is said about praying, but with doubtful and fluctuating hearts, and the very confidence the apostle requires is condemned.

The limiting clause is treated by everyone as the necessary condition rather than a restriction to be regretted. Barnes calls it the proper and necessary limitation of all prayer, since God has not promised anything contrary to his will and it could not be right that he should; no man who thought his own wishes a better guide than the will of God could hope for good, and it is one of the most desirable of all arrangements that the promise should be bounded in this way. Clarke identifies the will with what has been revealed: what God has promised in his word we are justified in expecting, and what he has promised and we expect we ought to pray for — so that faith and prayer are not boldly to advance claims on God, and we must take care that what we ask and believe for is agreeable to his revealed will. Robertson calls the phrase the secret of all prayer, true even in the case of Jesus himself, and adds that God hears us even when he does not give us what we ask, and particularly then. Wesley reads heareth as meaning favourably regards, and Henry sets the same boundary from the other side, that it is not fit we should ask what is contrary either to God’s majesty and glory or to our own good.
15: On what follows from being heard, Barnes is the most careful. To know that we have the petitions cannot mean that we already possess the thing asked for, since prayer often concerns what is future — protection on a journey, a harvest, recovery from illness, the safe return of a son from sea — none of which could be granted at once. It means rather that we shall have them, the argument resting on the faithfulness of God; and where the specific thing asked is not granted, the prayer is still not disregarded and what is most for our good will be given. Clarke reaches the same conclusion by a shorter route, that we may consider the petitions as sure as if we already had them and shall have them as soon as we need them, since God does not give today’s needed mercy tomorrow but gives it when it is needful. Henry states the comfort plainly, that to know one’s petitions are heard is as good as knowing they are answered, and Gill adds that God hears and answers all who ask according to his will. Robertson calls the sentence an amplification of the second limitation, notes that the perfect tenses give a confidence of possession by anticipation and make the asking itself an abiding thing, and takes the answer to be already had. Wesley says as much in a line, that faith anticipates the blessings and has the petitions even before the event, so that when the event comes we know it comes in answer to our prayer. Calvin denies the sentence is a superfluous repetition: what was declared generally about the success of prayer is now affirmed specially, that the godly ask nothing of God which they do not obtain. But he limits the claim in the same breath, since the petitions in view are right and humble ones consistent with the rule of obedience, the faithful not giving loose rein to their desires nor indulging whatever pleases them but always regarding in their prayers what God commands. The purpose of the repetition, he says, is to apply the general doctrine to each individual, so that no believer should doubt God is propitious to his own prayers, and may wait with a quiet mind until the Lord performs what he asks, casting the burden on God and so relieved of trouble and anxiety.
16:
Nobody claims to know for certain what the sin unto death is, and two make the uncertainty part of the comment. Barnes says opinion has been greatly diverse and is by no means settled, and rather than argue he lists what has been held: the sin against the Holy Ghost; any great and enormous sin such as murder or idolatry; a sin punishable by death under the law of Moses; a sin subjecting the offender to excommunication; a sin bringing fatal disease on him, as with those who abused the Lord’s Supper at Corinth; and offences against the civil law which the magistrate could neither pardon nor commute, so that prayer would be useless where the condemnation was just and proper where it was not. The bare list, he says, shows the difficulty of settling the sense and the impropriety of much confidence in one’s own judgment about it. Clarke sets out three chief opinions in the same spirit, beginning with a distinction he says the Jewish schools actually drew between a sin unto death, meaning one to which the law had assigned that punishment, and a sin not unto death, meaning transgressions of ignorance and inadvertence. His second is the civil one, that some crimes must be punished with death by statute and admit no pardon while others might be commuted at the magistrate’s discretion or at the intercession of powerful friends, so that pleading is useless in the first case and may prevail in the second — from which he draws the moral that men should feel for one another’s distresses and use their influence for the wretched.

Robertson accepts the distinction as real without narrowing it beyond what the text allows. Most sins are not mortal, he says, but John clearly conceives of one deadly enough to be called unto death; the distinction is common in the rabbinic writings, and the Greek Old Testament has a phrase for incurring a death-bearing sin. He notes the parallel distinction between sinning wilfully after full knowledge and sinning in ignorance, recalls the unpardonable sin of attributing the manifest work of the Holy Spirit to the devil, and suggests John may be applying that to men who reject Jesus as God’s Son and set themselves up as antichrists. Wesley defines it more narrowly still, as total apostasy from both the power and the form of godliness, while allowing a second sense, one which God has determined to punish with death. Gill approaches from the other end and defines the brother rather than the sin, as one judged born again, belonging to the household of God and under the watch and care of the saints.

Whether prayer is forbidden here is the sharpest disagreement of the passage. Wesley reads the clause as a prohibition and says so in as many words: the apostle does not say he shall pray for that, which means let him not pray for it. Robertson denies exactly this. John does not forbid praying in such cases; he simply does not command prayer for them, and leaves them to God. Henry stands between, holding that we cannot pray that the sins of the impenitent and unbelieving should be forgiven while they remain such, nor that mercy which presupposes forgiveness should be granted while they wilfully continue so, but that we may pray for their repentance and for their being enriched with faith in Christ, and on that ground for every other saving mercy. Calvin, who does not settle the identification either, is most concerned with the temper the passage might produce. He treats the falls of the brethren as stimulants to prayer and calls it an iron hardness to feel no pity when souls redeemed by Christ’s blood are going to ruin; and while recommending sympathy he warns against two things at once, the cruelty of condemning our brethren and an extreme rigour in despairing of their salvation.
17: The closing verse is read by most as a guard against the previous one. Barnes says it is thrown in to prevent the inference that because one enormous sin cannot be forgiven, sin as such is unpardonable: everything unrighteous is to be reckoned sin, but we are not to suppose all such sin is of a character that cannot be forgiven. Wesley states both halves in one line, that all deviation from perfect holiness is sin but not all sin is unpardonable. Gill illustrates from cases, that David’s sins were unrighteousness against both God and man and yet were put away, and that Peter sinned very foully and did great injustice to his Lord and was given repentance unto life. Robertson turns it outward, that the world today takes sin too lightly, even jokingly, as a mere animal inheritance, whereas sin is a terrible reality — though there is no cause for despair, since sin not unto death can be overcome in Christ. Calvin canvasses three ways of construing the sentence, adversatively, consecutively, or by taking the unrighteousness as complete unrighteousness and so the summit of sin, and declines to choose between the first two, leaving it to the reader’s judgment since the result is nearly the same. Clarke defines the term simply as every act contrary to justice, a transgression of the law which condemns all injustice. Barnes adds what the guard is for: there are many who commit sin whom we may hope to see recovered, and for those prayer may still be made, so that the acknowledgment of one unpardonable sin is not to be turned into a general despair. Gill presses his two examples for the same purpose, noting that in both the offence was real and grave and the wrath of God is revealed against all such unrighteousness, and yet in neither did it prove to be unto death, since repentance unto life was given and pardoning grace applied afresh. Wesley reaches the same conclusion from the other direction, since if all deviation from perfect holiness counts as sin then the category is far wider than the class of things that cannot be pardoned, and the wideness of the one is what makes the narrowness of the other bearable.
18:
How far the denial reaches is the first question, and the answers run from strict to very strict. Barnes qualifies it twice: the man born of God is not habitually and characteristically a sinner and does not ultimately sin and perish, and therefore cannot commit the unpardonable sin — though he may fall into sin and grieve his brethren, which is why we are never to stop praying for a true Christian or suppose he has put himself beyond the reach of our prayers. He treats the verse in its connection as full proof that a true Christian will never commit that sin and never fall from grace. Robertson reads the tense the same way, that the present means he does not keep on sinning. Calvin sets the limit from the other side and names those he is arguing against: if God’s children were supposed wholly free from all sin, as the fanatics contend, the apostle would contradict himself, since he has just enjoined mutual prayer among brethren. What is meant is that they do not wholly fall away from grace, and the faithful, though they fall through the infirmity of the flesh, groan under the burden of sin, loathe themselves and do not cease to fear God — and that, he says, is what it is not to sin. Clarke states the opposite without qualification, that this is spoken of adult Christians, who are cleansed from all unrighteousness and consequently from all sin. Wesley qualifies by duration rather than degree: so long as that loving faith abides in him he neither speaks nor does anything God has forbidden. Henry reads the security as extending precisely to the sin just discussed, since the new nature and the indwelling Spirit prevent the admission of unpardonable sin.

Who does the keeping is a straight textual disagreement. Gill, Clarke, Calvin, Wesley and Henry all take the believer to keep himself: Clarke glosses it as keeping himself in the love of God by building himself up on his most holy faith and praying in the Holy Ghost, Wesley as watching unto prayer, Calvin as keeping himself in the fear of God and not suffering himself to lose all sense of religion; and Henry says the clause indicates the power the regenerate have by virtue of their regeneration rather than merely describing a duty. Robertson dissents on the strength of the manuscripts, taking the participle as a first aorist passive referring to Christ and the object as him rather than himself, so that the sentence means Christ keeps the one begotten of God. He grants the phrase is difficult but notes that the two participles differ in form, that Jesus uses the same verb of himself elsewhere, and that he speaks in the same terms of keeping his disciples.

On the last clause the sense turns on how much force the verb carries. Robertson says it means to lay hold of or grasp rather than merely to touch superficially, and that the evil one here is masculine and personal, probably Satan and not any evil man. Calvin makes the same distinction in his own way: reference is made to a deadly wound, since the children of God do not remain untouched by Satan’s assaults but ward off his strokes with the shield of faith so that they do not penetrate the heart, and spiritual life is never extinguished in them. Barnes says the great enemy is repelled and the believer kept from falling into his snares; Wesley adds two words that supply the whole limitation, that he does not touch him so as to hurt him; and Henry reads it as meaning that the wicked one may not touch him unto death. Clarke explains why the attack fails, that the devil finds nothing of his own nature in such a man to work upon, Christ dwelling in his heart by faith.
19:
The certainty in the first clause is taken as real knowledge rather than a hope. Barnes says the apostle supposed true Christians might have evidence clear enough to leave no doubt in their own minds that they are the children of God. Gill specifies how that is known, by the Spirit witnessing to the spirits of the saints and by the fruits and effects of regenerating grace, love to the brethren among them. Clarke calls it the fullest proof of the truth of Christianity and of our own reconciliation to God through the death of his Son.

The second clause turns on a point of grammar, and three of them agree against the common rendering. Barnes explains that the Greek word may indeed be neuter, as the translators took it, meaning that the world lies in wickedness, but that it may equally be masculine and mean the wicked one, so that the whole world is under his control; and he gives two reasons for preferring the second, that the corresponding phrase in the next verse must be masculine, since it means being in him that is true, and that this reading makes better sense of the sentence. Robertson agrees that the word is masculine here as in the previous verse, and renders it that the world lies in the evil one. Clarke gives the same rendering and presses the figure hard: the world lies in the arms of the wicked one, fast asleep and carnally secure, deriving its heat and power from its infernal fosterer. He then asks whether the actions, tempers, opinions and maxims of worldly men do not prove it, and quotes Wesley’s remark that the horrible state of the world is painted here in the liveliest colours; on which he supplies his own commentary, that the actions of such men are opposed to the law of God, their conversation shallow and false, their contracts forced and deceitful, their quarrels ridiculous and ferocious, and their friendships hollow and fickle — all of it the effect of lying in those arms, since they become instinct with his own spirit. Robertson makes the same judgment historically rather than morally, calling the clause a terrible picture of the Graeco-Roman world of the first century, and notes that it is confirmed both by Paul and by the pagan satirists and historians of the period.

On the extent of the term everyone agrees. Barnes says the world here means not the material world but the people who dwell on the earth, taking in all idolaters and all sinners of every grade and kind. Gill and Calvin set the two halves of the verse against each other as the point of it, the certainty of the believer’s standing being stated precisely so that the condition of everything outside may be measured against it.
20:
What the understanding is gets a careful qualification from Barnes: not a faculty of the mind, since religion gives us no new faculties, but such instruction that we do in fact understand the truths in question — all correct knowledge of God being traced directly or indirectly to the great Prophet he has sent. Clarke calls it a more eminent degree of light than was ever enjoyed before, since he who lay in the Father’s bosom has declared him, together with a spiritual understanding by which we may know the true God. Wesley says the same in a phrase, a spiritual understanding by which we know the true one. Calvin makes the point structural: the children of God being assailed on every side, he now reminds them where their knowledge is especially to be found, since faith not really founded on God will never stand firm in the contest. He presses the adjective, that true here means not one who tells the truth but one who really is God, the word being set against what is fictitious and so distinguishing him from all idols; and he ascribes to Christ the office of illuminating our minds in the knowledge of God, since he is the only true image of the invisible God and the only interpreter of the Father. Gill lists what made the coming knowable, that the apostles saw and heard and handled him and that the prophetic marks were up. Robertson notes that the verb carries a perfect sense, that the noun for understanding occurs only here in these writings, and that being in him that is true stands in deliberate contrast with the world lying in the evil one.

How the two clauses relate is a small point with a large consequence. Robertson denies that the clause naming the Son stands in apposition to what precedes it, taking it rather as an explanation of how we are in the True One, namely by being in his Son; and he grants that grammatically the demonstrative which follows may refer either to Jesus Christ or to the True One. That is the crux, and Barnes gives it the fullest treatment. He acknowledges much difference of opinion over whether the words refer to the immediate antecedent or a more remote one, and comes down for the immediate: the writer who began by saying the Word was God, who recorded that all things were made by him, and who reported both the saying that the Father and the Son are one and the confession of Thomas, would apply this appellation to him. He adds an argument from the consequences of the other reading, that if the apostle did not mean this he used an expression liable to be misunderstood, and one that would lead men into the very sin he warns against in the next verse, the substituting of a creature in the place of God. If the reference is to Christ, Barnes says, it is a direct assertion of his divinity, since there could be no higher proof than to affirm that he is the true God. He records that many manuscripts and versions insert the word God in the clause, but that the reading is not well enough sustained to be adopted by the critical editors. Wesley states the same conclusion without argument, that this Jesus is the only living and true God together with the Father and the Spirit and the original fountain of eternal life, and notes with satisfaction that the beginning and the end of the epistle agree. Clarke reaches further, that it is through this revelation of Jesus that we know the Trinity in the undivided unity of the Godhead. Barnes closes on the last phrase, that Christ has life in himself and is the source of life to the soul, perhaps the appellation this apostle gives him most often.
21:
The address itself is noticed before the command. Clarke observes that the apostle closes with the same affectionate word he began with, and renders it beloved children; Barnes calls it a favourite mode of address with this writer and proper in a parting counsel which embraces everything he had to say, since his whole object had been to lead them to the knowledge and love of God, and all his counsels would be followed if nothing were allowed to estrange their hearts from him. Robertson notes that the reflexive is neuter to agree with the address, and that the active voice accents the need of effort on their part, idolatry being everywhere and the peril great.

How wide the prohibition runs is where they differ, and the difference is one of degree rather than direction. Barnes defines the word carefully: properly an image or spectre, then any figure representing something invisible, and so anything designed to represent God and set up to be acknowledged as representing him. On that definition it covers not only heathen deities but any image meant to represent the true God and through which he is to be adored, the essentials being a representation of the Deity and the making of it an object of worship. Gill begins with the heathen idols the readers lived among and the freedom taken in eating things sacrificed in their temples, then extends the word by stages: to images introduced by men who went by the name of Christians, to errors and false doctrines which are the figments of men’s minds, to the lusts of the heart, and finally to every creature loved too much, since covetousness is itself called idolatry. Wesley runs the same ladder in one sentence, from the worship of false gods to that of images or of any creature, and then to every inward idol, loving or fearing anything more than God. Clarke works it out as instruction: have no idols in your houses, none in your churches, none in your hearts; and his list of what may serve as one is deliberately mixed, running from pictures and relics and crosses to pleasure, wealth, fame, furniture, books, titles and human friendships — his rule being that a man’s idol is whatever he seeks his happiness from and whatever keeps him from finding his all in God. He adds the original occasion, that the apostle was cautioning his disciples against going with the heathen into the temples to eat of the feasts on the sacrifices, since to be present was to participate; and he records an old English version that rendered the word by a term for dolls, its translator having esteemed all images used in worship to be such.

Calvin presses the command furthest and turns it into a polemic. The apostle, he says, does not merely condemn idolatry but commands us to beware of all images and idols, which implies that the worship of God cannot remain uncorrupted wherever men begin to be in love with them; superstition is so innate in us that the least occasion infects us with its contagion. His figure is of fire: dry wood over coals will not catch so easily as idolatry lays hold of men when an occasion is given, and images are the sparks — or rather torches, enough to set the whole world alight. He extends the word beyond statues to altars and every instrument of superstition, and rejects as ridiculous any attempt to confine the verse to images of the pagan gods, since the apostle teaches generally that religion is corrupted whenever a bodily form is ascribed to God or statues and pictures form part of his worship. Gill closes where Calvin does, noting that the passage serves as an antidote against the image-worship later introduced, and that nothing in creation is to be loved more than God or Christ.
